articles.title: Global warming could make Russia richer. It could also bring NATO closer to its doorstep
articles.summary: The Earth is heating up, but things may not go all south for Russia if it looks north. For most of the world, global warming is a growing calamity.
articles.body: The Earth is heating up, but things may not go all south for Russia if it looks north.For most of the world, global warming is a growing calamity. But for Russia, the melting Arctic presents a more complicated picture. As rising temperatures threaten its environment and infrastructure, they could also open new shipping routes and access to resources long locked beneath the ice.The Arctic is warming more than three times faster than the rest of the world and may experience its first practically ice-free summer by 2030, according to the US department of defense's 2024 Arctic strategy.This rapid transformation is reshaping the region's strategic importance, as declining sea ice increases the viability of Arctic maritime transit routes and access to undersea resources.In 2025, commercial ships made more than 100 voyages along the Northern Sea Route and transported over three million metric tons of cargo, marking the highest figure on record.The frozen frontier is now becoming an increasingly accessible zone of geopolitical contest among major powers.Nato 7 vs Russian Arctic fortressOne of the Earth’s coldest regions is now becoming a military hotbed, with the US-aligned nations challenging Russia in a shared backyard.Speaking to the TOI, Prof Rajan Kumar, Professor at the School of International Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, pointed out the growing military tensions around the North Pole.“A key challenge in the Arctic is the growing militarisation and geopolitical contest as countries such as the US, Canada and Norway become more active around its rich resources”, Rajan said.Seven of the eight Arctic states, Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden and the United States, are now Nato members (with Finland and Sweden joining in 2023 and 2024 respectively), greatly enhancing the alliance's posture in the region.Only Russia remains outside the transatlantic alliance, creating what analysts describe as a "NATO 7 vs Russia" dynamic that has fundamentally altered Arctic security calculations.Moscow, on the other hand, maintains the largest Arctic territory and most developed regional military presence of all Arctic nations, as documented in the US department of defence Arctic strategy.According to an analysis by the Atlas Institute, Moscow has reactivated more than 50 Soviet-era military outposts across the Arctic since 2008, and built up the capabilities of its northern fleet based near Murmansk.The Kola Peninsula hosts about two-thirds of Russia's second-strike nuclear capabilities and is home to the northern fleet, which operates six of Russia's 12 nuclear-armed submarines, according to Reuters reporting based on IISS Military Balance 2025 data.Russia has deployed advanced S-400 surface-to-air missile systems to strategic locations such as Franz Josef Land and Novaya Zemlya, significantly expanding its anti-access capabilities in the region.As per Reuters, the country hosts the world’s largest icebreaker fleet, consisting of 42 vessels that support the operation of the Northern Sea Route.NATO has responded to this changing landscape with significant institutional and military investments. In February 2026, the alliance launched Arctic Sentry, a multi-domain enhanced Vigilance Activity strengthening deterrence and defence across the Arctic and High North, according to NATO. The alliance also opened a third Combined Air Operations Centre in Bodo, Norway, in October 2025, and established Forward Land Forces in Finland in June 2026.The Greenland questionGreenland has emerged as a focal point of Arctic competition, with its location between Europe and North America making it strategically important for both Europe and North America in defence and space operations.US President Donald Trump's interest in acquiring Greenland first became public in August 2019, but intensified significantly during his second term. In December 2024, President-elect Trump declared that "the ownership and control of Greenland is an absolute necessity", AP reported." The US laid its claim on Greenland because it saw the way the region’s politics was emerging”, Rajan said.“It wants to have a say in the region", he added.After months of diplomatic tension, including Trump's threats to use military force and impose tariffs on European nations, the US, Denmark and Greenland eventually signed a trilateral security agreement on 22 September 2026 at the UN General Assembly in New York.The agreement allows the US to "modernise and expand" operations at Pituffik Space Base (formerly Thule Air Base), establish two defence areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, and deploy the proposed "Golden Dome" missile defence system, according to CFR analysis.Yet, Russia’s growing military presence in the Arctic is only one aspect of the region’s changing strategic landscape. The warming that is making the Arctic more accessible also presents Moscow with economic opportunities and environmental challenges.Boon and baneFor Russia, climate change can look like an opportunity as well as a threat.The idea that Russia could benefit from climate change emerged from climate-impact research and economic projections, then became part of Russia’s political and strategic narrative about the Arctic.Its enormous northern territory, Arctic coastline and fossil-fuel reserves have encouraged hopes that warming could lower heating costs, expand agriculture and open new trade routes. Russia’s submission to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change says the country has warmed by about 0.47°C per decade since the mid-1970s, roughly 2.5 times the global rate.The most visible opportunity is the Northern Sea Route along Russia’s Arctic coast. Retreating sea ice has shortened transit times and made the route more accessible, potentially helping Russia export oil, gas and minerals to Asian markets. However, more traffic also means greater risks from accidents, oil spills, black-carbon emissions, underwater noise and invasive species.Navigation remains difficult because of mobile ice, inadequate charting, costly insurance and limited search-and-rescue infrastructure.According to Professor Rajan: “While climate change initially offers Russia some economic advantages, there are significant risks involved, such as frozen bacteria and viruses being released, and (global) warming impacting the Siberian region, river systems, and permafrost.”So, while Russia gains in some ways, it will also incur losses due to global warming, Rajan said.Agriculture presents a similarly mixed picture. Warmer conditions could lengthen growing seasons and permit cultivation farther north. Yet temperature alone does not create productive farmland: many northern areas have poor soils, weak transport links and unstable ground.Meanwhile, Russia’s existing agricultural heartlands face worsening heat and water stress. The Moscow Times reported that summer rainfall in some southern regions fell 25 per cent between 1976 and 2022. Without stronger global mitigation, Krasnodar, Rostov, Stavropol, Astrakhan and Kalmykia could experience an additional 13–26 extremely hot days annually by mid-century.Permafrost thaw may impose the highest direct cost. Reuters reports that permafrost covers 65 per cent of Russia and supports homes and infrastructure used by more than 15 million people. A leading Russian permafrost scientist quoted by Reuters estimated that continued warming could cause seven trillion rubles, about $97 billion, in infrastructure damage by 2050. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) projects that 69 per cent of fundamental Arctic infrastructure could be at risk by that year under a medium-emissions scenario, affecting more than 1,200 settlements, 36,000 buildings and four million people across the Arctic.Russia also faces an economic danger unrelated to physical warming: Global decarbonisation.The World Bank warns that declining demand for fossil fuels could reduce and destabilise Russian revenue from hydrocarbons and energy-intensive exports. It argues that Russia’s more durable opportunity lies in diversifying into renewable energy and other low-carbon industries rather than relying on continued fossil-fuel extraction.Russia could therefore secure limited gains from a warmer world, particularly in Arctic transport, heating and selected northern agriculture. But these benefits are conditional and uneven.Sberbank has estimated annual Russian climate damage could reach 580 billion rubles, or $6.7 billion, between 2023–2027.Indian stakes in the ArcticRussia’s efforts to turn a warming Arctic into an economic and strategic advantage also have implications for India. New Delhi’s 2022 Arctic Policy explicitly identifies the effects of melting ice on India’s economic, military and strategic interests, including global shipping routes, energy security and access to mineral resources.The policy rests on six pillars: Scientific research and cooperation; climate and environmental protection; economic and human development; transportation and connectivity; governance and international cooperation; and national capacity building.India is an observer in the Arctic Council and has established a research presence in Svalbard, including an atmospheric laboratory at Ny-Ålesund and a multi-sensor observatory in Kongsfjorden.Delhi’s policy also calls for greater participation in the Arctic Council and a better understanding of the region’s international laws, governance structures and geopolitics.But India’s interests extend beyond scientific research. The Northern Sea Route could offer an alternative to established shipping corridors during disruptions, although its distance from India and the challenges of Arctic navigation may limit its commercial appeal.“The Northern Sea Route could serve as an alternative if there are disruptions in the Suez Canal or the Red Sea. However, it is a much longer route for India compared with the Mediterranean route”, Rajan said.According to Professor Rajan, India could play a role, “either independently or in partnership with other countries”, in ensuring that the Northern Sea Route remains open and that no single country dictates access to it, in line with India's stance on freedom of navigation.The rising mercury may be opening new routes across the Arctic, but as the ice melts away, it reveals a new contest over access, influence and control.You use AI every day. articles.title: A former CIA agent is being ordered to forfeit $100 million in luxury Florida properties; investigators say his assets included four homes, gold bars, luxury watches and a car
articles.summary: Behind the walls of some of Florida’s most expensive homes, investigators say, lay a spending spree funded not by private wealth but by money allegedly
articles.body: Behind the walls of some of Florida’s most expensive homes, investigators say, lay a spending spree funded not by private wealth but by money allegedly siphoned from the US government. According to Yahoo News, a former senior CIA official now faces the loss of a multimillion-dollar property portfolio, gold bars and luxury possessions after admitting to a scheme that prosecutors say exploited the secrecy surrounding classified intelligence operations to defraud the federal government of approximately $194 million. David J. Rush, 49, has pleaded guilty to the scheme. Under the terms of his plea agreement, he must forfeit assets acquired through the fraud and repay the government, adds the report.A secret programme allegedly used to divert fundsAccording to Yahoo News, Rush held a senior executive-level position at the CIA and possessed a Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information security clearance, giving him access to highly classified activities. According to court documents, he also misrepresented his educational qualifications and military experience while advancing through government service.Prosecutors allege that Rush exploited his position by creating a fictitious Special Access Program, described in court records as SAP #1. Such programmes impose additional access restrictions beyond those associated with ordinary classified information, adds the online report.By presenting the fabricated programme as legitimate, Rush allegedly persuaded government contractors and subcontractors that their work served sensitive national security purposes. He also invoked restrictive need-to-know requirements that made it difficult for colleagues and other personnel to scrutinise his requests through routine administrative, contracting and financial checks, the report claims.$145 million channelled into luxury real estateAs part of the alleged scheme, Rush directed an independent subcontractor to establish a holding company and a corresponding bank account. The arrangement was presented as necessary to acquire South Florida properties for sensitive government purposes.A company holding a US government contract subsequently transferred approximately $145 million to the holding company at Rush’s direction. The money was then used for property acquisitions, renovations, improvements and contemplated resales, according to the case documents, informs the online report.The properties identified in the proceedings include four high-value acquisitions across Palm Beach and Hobe Sound, collectively worth more than $100 million.If we go by the report, the purchases comprised a parcel at 243 Seaspray Avenue in Palm Beach for $13.9 million in December 2025; a home at 236 Via Las Brisas for $22.9 million that same month; another property at 311 Polmer Park Road for $27 million in January 2026; and land at 511 South Beach Road in Hobe Sound for $40 million in February 2026.Gold bars, luxury watches and a BMWReal estate was only part of the assets investigators linked to the scheme, states the report. Rush also acquired 298 gold bars, luxury watches and two BMW vehicles, according to the allegations and plea agreement. Among the purchases was a BMW Alpina XB7 valued at approximately $172,232. Four of the luxury watches alone cost around $63,700, adds the online report.The forfeiture order targets the assets connected to the fraud, including the Florida properties and other valuables. The case illustrates the scale of the alleged misuse of public funds and the difficulty of detecting wrongdoing when ordinary financial oversight is deliberately obstructed.Intelligence secrecy under scrutinyThe case also highlights a vulnerability inherent in classified operations: the very restrictions designed to protect national security can complicate oversight when someone in a position of authority abuses them. FBI Director Kash Patel condemned Rush’s conduct in a public statement, emphasising the betrayal of government responsibilities and public trust.With his guilty plea, Rush faces the financial consequences of the scheme through asset forfeiture and restitution. The proceedings serve as a reminder that even within highly secretive institutions, access and authority do not place individuals beyond financial scrutiny or the reach of the law.Images Courtesy: RealtorReady to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Dad and son remain critical after masked men attack in Leicestershire village
articles.summary: Leicestershire Police say the attack at the family home appeared "completely unprovoked".
articles.body:
A father and son are in hospital in a life-threatening condition after an attack in their family home which appeared "completely unprovoked", police have said.

Officers were called to reports of a disturbance at a house in Station Road , Thurnby, shortly before 00:30 BST on Thursday.

Leicestershire Police said a man in his 50s was stabbed multiple times, while a boy, 15, was also stabbed by two masked men who entered the property. The force gave an update on Friday to say both remained critical in hospital.

Officers added that the man's wife - who is in her 40s - suffered minor injuries to her hand and shoulder during the attack. Three other children who were in the address were not injured.

In the interest of public and police safety, police said armed officers were deployed but the men had left the house prior to them arriving.

The force added an investigation, led by the East Midlands Special Operations Unit (EMSOU), to understand the circumstances and motive would continue over the weekend.

Police said it would remain in the area as officers undertook searches for anything that may help them to understand and identify those responsible.

Det Insp Lorna Granville said: "This was a violent attack against a family in their own home which appears to have been completely unprovoked.

"Our investigation to understand what happened and why - and identify those behind such a horrific criminal act - is going to continue over the weekend.

"I'm making a direct appeal to people in Thurnby and the surrounding communities to come forward with any information if they haven't already done so.

"We owe it to the victims to locate the perpetrators and bring them to justice."

Granville added: "I'd like to speak to anyone who may have seen or heard anything suspicious, unusual or untoward in the area of Station Road and Somerby Road between 23:00 on Wednesday and the early hours of yesterday morning.

"This includes anyone who was driving in the area and captured anything on a dashcam or anyone with CCTV or doorbell footage.

"Anything you're able to provide, no matter how insignificant you think it might be, could help us."

The force said it had set up a major incident public portal for the public to submit information.

Simon Galton, councillor for Thurnby and Houghton, said he was "absolutely appalled" to hear of the attack on Thursday.

"Thurnby is a quiet place, yes we have anti-social behaviour, but we don't have serious violent crime of this nature.

articles.title: JONATHAN TURLEY: France's free speech crackdown shows what happens when politicians define truth
articles.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron declared American free speech is "the opposite of free speech," exposing France's deepening and dangerous censorship.
articles.body: French President Emmanuel Macron went full Orwell recently. While long the darling of Western media, Macron has been one of the most anti-free-speech leaders in the world. On Sept. 29, he declared that "The so-called American ‘free speech’ today, which some people have promoted, is the opposite of free speech." Having Emmanuel Macron holding forth on free speech is akin to Joey Chestnut proselytizing on veganism. France has been in a headlong plunge into censorship and speech criminalization. These laws criminalize speech under vague standards referring to "inciting" or "intimidating" others based on race or religion. For example, fashion designer John Galliano was found guilty in a French court on charges of making antisemitic comments in a Paris bar in 2010 and 2011. MACRON TRASHES AMERICAN FREE SPEECH AS RIOTS GRIP FRANCE — INTERNET UNLOADS: ‘ENORMOUS FOOL’ In another case, the father of French conservative presidential candidate Marine Le Pen was fined because he had called people from the Roma minority "smelly" in 2013. A French teenager was charged for criticizing Islam as a "religion of hate" in 2020. Many of us were disgusted recently when Macron celebrated Brigitte Bardot's life as someone who "embodied a life of freedom." As I discussed, the French government repeatedly prosecuted Bardot for speaking about her views. FRANCE BECOMES FIRST EU NATION TO BAN SOCIAL MEDIA FOR CHILDREN UNDER 15 Macron’s praise for Bardot’s "life of freedom" is reminiscent of the reaction of French officials to the massacre of editors at Charlie Hebdo, a satirical magazine. After hounding the victims for years with criminal investigations, the French government organized a march for free speech. As predicted, it then used the killing by Islamic extremists to further crack down on free speech. In my book "The Indispensable Right," I discuss how France has careened down the slippery slope of censorship for decades, and the desire to silence others has now become an insatiable appetite. UK ‘IN FREE FALL’ ON FREE SPEECH, EXPERT WARNS AS BRITISH MP BRANDS TRUMP ADMIN GRANT 'MAGA MONEY MEDDLING' Macron has supported figures like his anti-free-speech ally Thierry Breton in globalizing the reach of the infamous Digital Services Act (DSA) to curtail speech, including Americans and American companies. In his latest pitch for censorship, Macron pulls out an old saw that if everyone can speak freely, no one can speak freely. BIBLE VERSE LEADS TO TRIAL IN EUROPE. GROWING CRACKDOWN THREATENS OUR US-UK VALUES Macron declared that: "There is no freedom if there is no limit to my freedom, which begins with the freedom of others and respect for a common framework. I know this when I walk down the street: my freedom cannot mean hitting you, insulting you or trashing the public space we all share." That line is remarkably telling. It captures how even "insulting" language is treated as a crime in France. UK LAWMAKER WARNS IT’S ‘OPEN SEASON’ ON CHRISTIANS AS HE SOUNDS ALARM OVER ‘TWO-TIER JUSTICE’ Since then, France has been a leader in the rollback of free speech in the West, with ever-widening laws curtailing free speech. France regularly charges people for political and religious speech, including comedians and those criticizing the police. Many of us were disgusted recently when Macron celebrated Brigitte Bardot's life as someone who "embodied a life of freedom." As I discussed, the French government repeatedly prosecuted Bardot for speaking about her views. Macron's visceral reaction to free speech is shared by many in the European Union. ERDOGAN'S TURKEY CRACKS DOWN ON LGBT COMMUNITY IN NAME OF PRESERVING FAMILY VALUES I spoke in Berlin at the World Forum, which boasted the slogan, "A New World Order with European Values." Former President Bill Clinton and his wife, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, and other Americans cheered on the European efforts. The Digital Services Act bars speech that is viewed as "disinformation" or "incitement." When it was passed over the condemnations of many of us in the free speech community, European Commission Executive Vice President Margrethe Vestager celebrated by declaring that it is "not a slogan anymore — that what is illegal offline should also be seen and dealt with as illegal online. Now it is a real thing. Democracy’s back." JONATHAN TURLEY: COMEY’S SHELL POST MAY BE CRASS, BUT CHARGING HIM IS A FREE SPEECH TRAP Despite his unpopularity in France, Macron remains a favorite of the establishment and the media in the United States. I was appalled years ago when he came to Congress to spread his anti-free speech gospel. Macron called for a joint war against "fake news" and declared, "Democracy is about true choices and rational decisions. The corruption of information is an attempt to corrode the very spirit of our democracies." Our representatives applauded like seals with little recognition that he was referencing censorship. Macron believes that he should be able to dictate which views are "corrosive" to the spirit of democracy. LEGAL EXPERTS WARN COMEY ‘86 47’ INDICTMENT FACES FIRST AMENDMENT HURDLES The claim that more speech means less speech is an oxymoronic talking point of the anti-free-speech movement. As I discussed in my book, there has not been a single censorship system in history that has worked to kill a single idea or movement. Instead, it has given more power to politicians like Macron to silence critics and intimidate opponents. In the end, the only true solution to bad speech is better speech. The public can sort out its own values and weigh opposing views without the strict guidance of the government. Free speech serves as its own disinfectant. Ultimately, allowing people not just free inquiry, but free expression bends the arc of humanity toward truth. Hate and prejudice are inherently flawed values that tend to collapse when exposed to full, robust debate. articles.title: Llanon 'tropical jungle' must relocate after neighbours complain
articles.summary: James Wale moved to the site two years ago and keeps animals including wallabies and rare birds.
articles.body:
A man who lives in a log cabin and keeps wallabies, mongooses, porcupines, parrots and other rare birds has been told to move.

James Wale relocated to the rural Carmarthenshire site two years ago, having previously run a rare bird business in Pembrokeshire.

Neighbours said the site sounded like a "tropical jungle", especially at night.

Carmarthenshire Council issued Wale with an enforcement notice alleging he had broken planning rules, but he has been given more time to relocate the animals.

Planning agents representing the bird enthusiast said he wanted to create a "major tourism venture", and that his former business in the grounds of Picton Castle ended because the lease was not renewed.

Wale moved to the 17-acre woodland near Llannon and had hoped to set up an owl garden centre, but scaled back his plans to create a private bird welfare home along with some forestry and farming activities.

As well as the exotic animals, Wale also kept horses, goats, chickens and ducks, according to the enforcement appeal.

Documents said the abandoned venture planned to include "reptile, mongoose and several animal enclosures".

A planning application was then prepared for a smaller-scale venture including about 30 bird and animal enclosures, with Wale not intending to live onsite.

Two enforcement notices were issued by the council last year, one of which was withdrawn, and another sent this year which told him to stop living on the land, remove the cabin and stop keeping non-agricultural birds and animals.

During the subsequent appeal, seven objectors expressed concerns about the changes at the land linked to sanitation, stray animals and unusual noises.

One objector said the noises were "not those of native species".

Another claimed the noise "often sounds like a tropical jungle" which, along with the sound of generators and dog-barking, was "particularly troublesome late at night".

A further comment said the site had become waterlogged, turning a "once beautiful forest" into a "fly-tipping incident".

The person submitted a photo of goats and a Labrador to the council and said they had strayed onto their land.

Llannon councillor Llinos Mai Davies claimed the site adversely affected neighbouring properties and had a negative impact on the character of the area.

Photos of the land were submitted showing the boggy conditions and the woodland access track off the A476.

A planning inspector appointed by Welsh ministers has now dismissed the appeal after seeing the cabin during a visit to the land.

"The appellant keeps a few chickens, ducks and horses on site along with a variety of more unusual animals including eagles, falcons, parrots, hornbills, mongooses, skunks, porcupine and wallaby," they said.

The inspector said there was a minor element of forestry and agricultural activity taking place, but that the main operation was of a "fundamentally different character" and unauthorised.

Wale should be given 12 rather than six months to stop using the land to keep non-agricultural animals, remove the enclosures and restore the site to its original condition, the inspector concluded.

"Given the unusual type and mix of the animals, it may well take more time to find a suitable alternative location," they added.

Wale also has 12 months to stop living on the land, remove the cabin and its associated foul drainage.

His agents told the Local Democracy Reporting Service that a planning application would be drawn up in a bid to keep the birds on site.

articles.title: Crookes named sixth coolest UK neighbourhood by Time Out magazine
articles.summary: Crookes is branded the country's sixth coolest suburb by Time Out magazine.
articles.body:
What makes a modern suburb trendy? Lots of places to eat and drink, perhaps? A youthful and vibrant population? Are live music venues and good leisure facilities a must?

After Crookes, in the west of Sheffield, was named the sixth coolest neighbourhood in the UK by Time Out magazine, the BBC spoke to people in the area to find out what they think makes the area so great.

Its offering of restaurants, cafes and bars was part of the rationale, while residents and business owners said the neighbourhood's independent style and tight-knit community are what make it so "cool".

Maurice Champeau has run the Crookes Social Club, a venue that regularly hosts gigs and events, for 15 years.

"I'm not really surprised to be honest with you because we've got a cracking little community in Crookes," he says when asked about the ranking.

"We recognise each other's faces. It's almost a village within the city," he added.

While the Mulehouse Road venue is a longstanding feature of the neighbourhood, serving as a working men's club from 1919, the high street has changed over the last decade.

Cloud Coffee is a speciality coffee shop that moved into the area in 2023.

"We wouldn't be anywhere else in the city. We love it up here," owner Connor Sadler said.

"Best neighbourhood on earth, isn't it? Can't believe we only finished sixth," the 27-year-old added.

Time Out magazine's Daniel Wray, who himself lives in the Norfolk Park area of Sheffield, says Crookes has become a "food and drink" hotspot.

"I've just noticed over the last few years every time I go there there seems to be something new there - a cafe or a bakery," he explains.

"It's quite understated and quiet, it's not that flashy. For such a concentrated area there's loads going on."

Ellie Gillis, 26, is a manager at the Punch Bowl pub. She recognises that Crookes has changed over the last few years.

"It's not always had the coolest of reputations," she said.

"People come in here and say this used to be so dodgy, but everything's changed.

"It's gone from being somewhere where it was maybe just students and older people to somewhere where there are all walks of life."

Deborah Clarke, 63, who is catching up with her friend Wendy Hueue on a walk down the busy high street, has also seen the transformation.

"I lived here all my life and it's completely changed for the better," she says.

"It has come up in the world, hasn't it?"

University of Sheffield student Georgia Wilson, 21, moved to the area in July, enticed by its "funky" cafes and busy atmosphere.

For Georgia, Crookes' coolness can be attributed to students.

"I think Sheffield Uni itself attracts a cool student population, it's gonna have to be a bit cool because everyone here's cool," she says.

For others, its the sense of community that makes them value the neighbourhood.

"We've got so many lovely shops, we've got a wonderful high street but I think what's also really important is how socially-minded lots of shops and independent businesses are," Crookes and Crosspool councillor Minesh Parekh says.

Luke Williams, who runs Williams and Co estate agency, says property prices in the area have "increased astronomically" over the last decade.

"The last property we sold in Crookes was viewed 35 times and sold for £30,000 over the asking price," he says. "The demand is there."

"I think it's an area where you have the best of both worlds. It's a buzzy area with a really nice community feel, but within five or 10 minutes you can be out in the Peak District.

"It's got good proximity to schools, hospitals and the universities."

articles.title: Masked robbers steal wine worth over $5m from top Italian vineyard
articles.summary: Masked thieves broke into a warehouse in Cortona, Italy and made off with around 30,000 bottles of wine from the prestigious Marchesi Antinori vineyard worth more than $5 million, in what the company says could rank among the largest wine thefts ever reported.
articles.body: Masked thieves broke into a warehouse in Cortona, Italy and made off with around 30,000 bottles of wine from the prestigious Marchesi Antinori vineyard worth more than $5 million, in what the company says could rank among the largest wine thefts ever reported. The thieves disarmed the alarm system to carry out the daring heist, which took place at the weekend, but was only discovered on Monday when workers arrived to prepare the wine for export, Antinori’s CEO Renzo Cotarella told CNN on Friday. The stolen wines were all from 2023 and include some of the winery’s most sought-after labels that retail for between €150 and €500 ($168 and $561) internationally. “Solaia, and Guado al Tasso, and Tignanello are the most icon(ic) wines we have,” said Cotarella, describing them as category-defining examples of the famous “Super Tuscan” red wines of the region. Between 60,000 and 70,000 bottles of Solaia are produced each year, and the thieves took around 10,000 bottles. No arrests have yet been made. Cortona police said they were conducting an extensive manhunt, but would not say whether they believe the two trucks used to steal the wine were still in Italy. “Given the scale of the theft, both in terms of the number of bottles stolen and their estimated market value, the incident may rank among the largest wine thefts ever reported,” Marchesi Antinori said in a statement. “The investigation by the competent authorities is ongoing, as are the assessments required to determine the precise extent of the theft.” Cotarella said the company is urging consumers not to purchase these wines from unknown sellers, and to report it if any appear on the market. Because the wine was in the warehouse to be shipped out, it was boxed and packaged, making it easier for the thieves to remove. The heist follows a string of other wine thefts. Last month 3,000 bottles of Barolo worth around €400,000 were stolen from the Conterno Fantino vineyard in Piedmont. It is unclear if the thefts are connected. Marchesi Antinori was founded in 1385 and is currently run by the 26th generation of the family. It exports to 170 countries and has annual revenues of around €265 million. Cotarella said he believes the wine will be found. “Two trucks cannot just disappear. I remain always positive,” he said.

articles.title: In 2021, a South Carolina couple started an HVAC company with $2,000 after losing their jobs; five years later, they say the business is on track to generate more than $8 million in annual revenue
articles.summary: A South Carolina couple who lost their jobs during the Covid started an air-conditioning business with just $2,000.
articles.body: A South Carolina couple who lost their jobs during the Covid started an air-conditioning business with just $2,000. Stephanie Postell and her husband, David Postell, founded Anchor Heating and Air in 2021 after being fired in December 2020. Nearly five years later, the company is on track to generate more than $8 million in annual revenue, according to Stephanie's account on the Blue Collar StartUp podcast.Both had years of experience in the heating and air-conditioning industry, but starting their own company meant working with limited resources. They used their $2,000 to purchase equipment and began taking on jobs independently.The company, Anchor Heating and Air, now provides heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) services in Charleston, South Carolina, and surrounding areas. In a podcast episode released September 9, Stephanie explained how they built the business and managed its growth.The couple also had to adjust to working together as business partners. Stephanie had previously been David's boss, but their new venture required them to share ownership and divide responsibilities according to their strengths.Starting with $2,000Before launching Anchor Heating and Air, Stephanie and David had spent several years in the industry. According to their company's website, they brought more than 30 years of combined experience when they started the business in 2021.They had also helped build an earlier HVAC company that reached $5 million in revenue within 20 months. However, losing their jobs in December 2020 meant starting again.Rather than purchasing an existing business, they established their own company with $2,000 for equipment. Stephanie said they reinvested the money earned from their first HVAC job into securing the next opportunity.They gradually expanded their services, which included air-conditioning repairs, maintenance and replacement, along with other heating and cooling solutions.How the couple divided workAs the business grew, Stephanie and David decided to handle separate responsibilities and not manage everything together.While David took charge of the technical side, Stephanie focused on marketing and operations. This allowed both to concentrate on areas where they had experience.Stephanie said they avoided interfering in each other's responsibilities. The arrangement was particularly important because she had previously been David's boss, whereas they were now equal business partners.They also agreed to keep personal disagreements out of the workplace. Stephanie explained that they did not want employees to feel uncomfortable or worry about arguments between their bosses.Children joined the businessThe family connection extended to the company when some of the couple's children worked there at different times. According to Stephanie, one child worked for approximately a year, while another stayed for up to four years.However, the couple maintained the same workplace rules for family members and other employees. Their children were expected to meet the same standards regarding performance, responsibilities and time off.Stephanie said they wanted to avoid preferential treatment and ensure employees were treated fairly, regardless of their relationship with the owners.Keeping work-life balanceOutside the business, Stephanie and David share an interest in off-roading. They spend weekends riding side-by-side off-road vehicles, travelling and visiting off-road parks.Stephanie said the hobby allows them to spend time together without constantly discussing work, schedules or business problems.This separation has become part of how they manage their relationship while running the company. They try to maintain a professional environment at work while making time for shared activities outside it.How the company reached $8 millionDuring the interview, Stephanie identified several factors behind the company's growth, including appropriate pricing, understanding finances, building a recognisable brand and hiring capable employees.She also stressed the importance of explaining heating and cooling options to customers instead of using high-pressure sales tactics.The company's website states that customers receive information about available solutions and prices before work begins, allowing them to choose services suited to their requirements.Stephanie also discussed investing in employees and establishing processes that support expansion. She said contractors need to charge enough for their services to sustain their businesses and support their workforce.Nearly five years after its launch, Anchor Heating and Air was on track to generate slightly more than $8 million in revenue during its fifth year, according to Stephanie. articles.title: Bangladesh’s mango diplomacy with India has reached its limits
articles.summary: Cultural gestures have kept relations from collapsing, but repairing ties with India will require tough negotiations.
articles.body:
For two years, Dhaka has deployed a soft diplomatic arsenal of prized Haribhanga mangoes, hilsa fish, jamdani fabrics, and Tangail sarees to keep its relationship with New Delhi from freezing into permanent estrangement. These gestures kept doors open, preserved public channels, and prevented temporary friction from decaying into absolute hostility.

Yet, as the dust settles, a cold geopolitical reality remains visible. Soft power can create an opening, but it cannot settle the hard politics waiting behind it. There comes an inevitable point in every strained diplomatic relationship when the mangoes have simply done all they can.

Since the mass uprising that began in Bangladesh in July 2024 and toppled Sheikh Hasina’s increasingly authoritarian rule of 15 years, Bangladesh has sought to avoid sharp confrontation with India. The instruments chosen by Dhaka were conspicuously soft.

Cultural programmes, textile exhibitions, hilsa festivals and trade gestures were paired with a determined effort by the Bangladeshi High Commission in New Delhi to keep talking to Indian counterparts, even when the respective governments had little pleasant to say to each other. This campaign was not entirely pointless. It was merely incapable of bearing the political weight eventually demanded of it.

A basket of mangoes can generate a momentary thaw. A saree exhibition can fill a grand room with appreciative visitors. A shipment of the coveted silvery delicacy of hilsa can evoke profound nostalgic warmth in Kolkata. None of these things, however, can determine the fate of Hasina, settle disputes over shared river waters, rebuild shattered political trust, or address the core security anxieties of two tightly interconnected neighbouring states.

That fundamental distinction – between keeping a diplomatic relationship alive and actually repairing its broken core – now defines the delicate balance between Bangladesh and India.

The limits of this approach were demonstrated clearly in 2025. In July, Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus’s erstwhile interim administration dispatched 1,000 kilograms (2,200 pounds) of high-grade Haribhanga mangoes to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, alongside additional consignments for senior officials and political leaders across New Delhi.

The gesture was interpreted as a deliberate signal that Dhaka sought normal, functional ties despite the intense bitterness that followed Hasina’s overthrow and her subsequent flight to Indian soil. The mangoes arrived swiftly on schedule. The heavy political problems remained exactly where they were.

Hasina remained in India while authorities in Dhaka pursued her formal extradition. The two capitals argued persistently over border management, transit rights, and the treatment of Bangladeshi citizens. Visa services, long a bellwether of bilateral warmth, were suspended and later resumed after Tarique Rahman’s BNP came to power in February this year. But the number of visas issued has still not returned to pre-2024 levels.

Unresolved questions concerning shared water resources, bilateral trade imbalances, and regional security continued to linger without resolution. Soft diplomacy was, at best, a pleasing sweetener rather than the main course.

Few pursued this softer strategy more visibly than Bangladesh’s outgoing envoy in New Delhi, M Riaz Hamidullah. Under his leadership, the High Commission experimented energetically with cultural outreach. The first jamdani exposition in Delhi, held in September 2025, brought traditional Bangladeshi weaving into an Indian artistic space where shared history was obvious.

In April 2026, the mission mounted another exhibition displaying 300 handloom sarees sourced directly from master weavers in Tangail and Pabna. The response from the Indian capital was positive.

As for cultural diplomacy, the initiative was a success. Indian connoisseurs arrived in droves, designers exchanged ideas, and sarees sold out within 24 hours. The shared Bengali cultural inheritance proved far easier to discuss than shared rivers. There was sound logic behind this tactic: building constituencies within Indian society who did not view Bangladesh strictly through the lens of immediate political quarrels provided a crucial buffer.

The diplomatic mistake lies in confusing access with real influence. A sold-out textile exhibition proves Indian admiration for Bangladeshi craftsmanship; it does not indicate agreement with Dhaka’s strategic posture. Cultural familiarity has never guaranteed political convergence in South Asia.

If it did, Dhaka and Kolkata would have settled every bilateral disagreement over hilsa-laden lunch decades ago. Indeed, even the fabric eventually ran into politics when the Tangail exhibition became entangled in contentious debates over heritage claims and geographical indication status.

Atmospherics inevitably run out of room. Sooner or later, formal political engagement must take over. Nothing illustrates this shift better than the continuing efforts to arrange a visit by Tarique Rahman to New Delhi. India extended invitations for both a direct bilateral visit and attendance at the BRICS summit in his capacity as chair of BIMSTEC.

Rahman did not make the journey. Dhaka noted that a high-level summit required an appropriate environment and mutual respect, while Indian officials publicly underscored that invitations had been extended without producing a visit.

This polite impasse revealed the true state of affairs. A prime ministerial visit requires a substantive agenda, careful political preparation, and deliverable outcomes that both leaders can sell to domestic audiences. India’s high commissioner in Dhaka, Dinesh Trivedi, has repeatedly urged direct top-level dialogue, emphasising that direct contact between leaders is necessary to resolve outstanding issues.

Soft diplomacy operates best when the underlying strategic foundation is already functional. When two governments agree on the fundamentals, cultural affinity adds warmth and colour. When they clash over fundamental interests, soft power can prevent complete rupture, but it cannot negotiate the terms of reconciliation.

India’s previous relationship with Dhaka rested on deep security cooperation, energy links, and established political arrangements. Hasina’s removal dismantled that comfortable architecture.

The leadership in Dhaka now demands a new equilibrium based strictly on sovereignty, reciprocity, and strategic flexibility. New Delhi maintains its own sharp concerns regarding regional security and Dhaka’s shifting external alignments.

These are complex matters involving trade treaties, water allocation, border enforcement, and intelligence cooperation. They cannot be managed by cultural envoys or resolved over dinner menus.

The gestures of the past two years were not failures; they preserved vital space during a turbulent political transition. But symbolism is now yielding diminishing returns. Both capitals understand that the next phase of South Asian geopolitics cannot be stitched together with fabric or negotiated over fruit. The mangoes succeeded in keeping the diplomatic door open. Real political bargaining must now walk through it.

articles.title: Is a bath sheet really different from a regular bath towel?
articles.summary: Bath sheets are becoming more popular, but are they any different than regular towels? I spoke with experts to find out more.
articles.body: With all the content available online these days, it can be hard to figure out what’s real and what’s hype. While we don’t always have the answers, we have a direct line to people who do — which is why we present to you our series The Internet Made Me Ask, where we have experts break down the truth about some of the buzziest trends (and questions) on our timelines, like how often should you wash makeup brushes. The first step in making sure your bathroom is fully equipped is getting a great set of plush bath towels that’ll hold up well over time. While shopping for a new set, however, you may see options for bath sheets, and wonder what exactly is a bath sheet and how is it any different from a regular bath towel? Is it just a huge towel, or does it have some sort of feature that warrants being called something different? I had the same questions, so I spoke to fabric experts to learn more about the similarities and differences between bath sheets and bath towels. I also recommend bath sheets from trusted NBC Selected brands for anyone convinced that they need to add some to their linen closet. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. What is a bath sheet? In general, a bath sheet is a really big towel, oftentimes with a length between 65 and 70 inches. In terms of the material, bath sheets and bath towels aren’t that much different. “A bath sheet is all about that oversized feel,” says Lindsey Johnson, CEO and co-founder of towel brand Weezie*. A bath sheet is sort of like if you combined a regular bath towel and a small blanket, so it’s ideal for people who like being wrapped up entirely after they come out of the shower or bath. Because they have more fabric, bath sheets can take longer to dry and are often more expensive than regular towels. *Any inclusion of Weezie in this story was made independent of Johnson, who we only consulted for shopping tips and guidance. We did not ask Johnson for product recommendations, though she does directly benefit from any Weezie purchase made from this story. What’s the difference between a bath sheet and a bath towel? There a few key differences between bath sheets and bath towels, here’s what experts say you should expect: Size: The main, and most noticeable difference between a bath sheet and a towel is the size. Bath sheets are much larger than traditional bath towels, sometimes making them feel more like bedding. Drying time: As Johnson mentioned above, a bath sheet will take a longer time to dry than a towel since it’s larger in length and width. This is something to consider when shopping for bath sheets, since a humid bathroom can prevent towels from drying quickly. Thickness and weight: While it depends on the particular bath sheet and how a brand differentiates it from its towels, bath sheets sometimes come in different thicknesses or GSM (grams per square meter) compared to their towel equivalent. Since they take a long time to dry, some brands make them in a lighter weight or thickness, according to Johsnon. In some instances, you can buy bath sheets and other matching towels to create a set. These bath sheets, which are made from 100% Turkish cotton, are available either as a set of two or four. They’re available in several solid shades, as well as a few stylish striped options. Shoppers say they appreciate how soft and plush the bath sheets are while also being absorbent. They’re safe to machine wash in cold water and tumble dry on low heat, according to the brand. This bath sheet from Weezie is made from 100% long-staple cotton, which makes for a softer feel, according to Preeti Arya, associate professor at the Fashion Institute of Technology. While it’s only available in white, the oversized towel comes with the option to monogram it in another color, with matching trim (so it would also make a great gift). These popular towels are made from a mix of cotton and fibers from bamboo, also called viscose, which makes them particularly soft and absorbent, according to the brand. They’re made with a “zero-twist” formation, meaning that the fibers aren’t twisted very tightly, which ultimately makes the bath sheet feel softer and work better at absorbing moisture from the body, according to Cozy Earth. The bath sheets have more than 475 five-star reviews (at the time of publishing), with shoppers saying they’re very soft and get even softer after they’ve been washed. Are bath sheets worth it? It depends on what you want out of a bath sheet or bath towel. If you enjoy being able to be completely covered by a plush towel, whether from a coziness standpoint or otherwise, then you should try out a bath sheet. If you don’t care much for that and just need a towel to dry you off, then it’s best to just get a regular towel and save some money. It’s important to get a bath sheet that is absorbent and made from a material that dries relatively fast if possible. If your towels already take a long time to dry, using something that takes just as long but that takes up even more space may not be ideal, especially since experts I spoke to about how often you should wash your towels recommend using two towels per week and trading off between uses. You may not be prepared to hang two gigantic towels in your space. Though, a towel warmer rack could help with this. What material should you get a bath sheet in? “I recommend looking into the fiber content. If you choose natural fiber, no matter what the weave type is, it will dry the water from your skin due to absorption,” says Arya. Arya recommends natural fibers like pima, Turkish and Egyptian cotton, which are all types of long-staple cotton (cotton bolls with particularly long fibers, which makes fabrics softer than traditional cotton). Additionally, you can consider linen, which is made from flax seeds, and hemp, made from hemp seeds, good options for a bath sheet that has absorption. articles.title: In 1943, Olympic skier Betty Woolsey began building a Wyoming ranch near Jackson Hole; its 270 acres were later protected from development through a conservation easement
articles.summary: Long before Jackson Hole became a destination for skiers and visitors drawn to the American West, Betty Woolsey was looking for somewhere quieter.
articles.body: Long before Jackson Hole became a destination for skiers and visitors drawn to the American West, Betty Woolsey was looking for somewhere quieter. An accomplished skier and mountaineer, she had competed internationally, climbed in the European Alps and travelled through remote mountain countries. Yet the place she chose to settle was a stretch of Wyoming land near Wilson, where she could ski uncrowded slopes, ride into the wilderness and build a working ranch. Woolsey began acquiring land for Trail Creek Ranch in the early 1940s, eventually making it her permanent home. By the time she died in 1997, aged 88, the property had become more than a ranch. About 270 acres were protected under a conservation easement.Betty Woolsey’s early life and mountaineering adventures in Europe and North AmericaWoolsey was born in Albuquerque, New Mexico, on 28 December 1908. Her father worked for the US Forest Service, and her early childhood included life in a log house overlooking the Sandia Mountains. The landscape left a lasting impression. After the family moved to New Haven, Connecticut, with five daughters, Woolsey went on to graduate from Vassar College.Her interest in mountains took her across the Atlantic. In the early 1930s, she travelled to Chamonix, France, where she climbed the Grépon, a granite peak that introduced her to the exposed routes of serious Alpine climbing. In Switzerland, she climbed Monte Rosa with the guide Bernhardt Biner, reaching a summit from which the Matterhorn and surrounding peaks were visible.She later explored North American mountain ranges with members of the American Alpine Club, an organisation she would belong to for 62 years. Her climbs included the Big Horn Mountains in Wyoming and the Canadian Rockies around Banff. She also joined an expedition to Mount Waddington in British Columbia, then regarded as Canada's highest unclimbed peak.A ski racer who competed at the 1936 OlympicsWoolsey's mountain experience extended beyond climbing. She learnt to ski in Europe and developed into a competitive downhill racer, eventually representing the United States at the 1936 Winter Olympics. Her fellow team members selected her as captain, and she was the leading American skier in the Olympic downhill event.The Games took place as the “Nazi Olympics”. The racing continued after the event, alongside her friend Marian “Sis” McKean, as the two competed against experienced European skiers.Woolsey's strongest domestic result came three years later. In 1939, she won the US National Downhill Championship at Mount Hood, Oregon. By then, Sun Valley in Idaho had become a centre of American ski culture, attracting racers from Europe as well as well-known figures from Hollywood. Woolsey spent time there, but the resort lifestyle eventually lost its appeal.Finding a permanent home near Jackson HoleWoolsey travelled to the Jackson Hole area with friends and was drawn to the terrain around Teton Pass. In 1943, she began acquiring the Wyoming land that would become Trail Creek Ranch. The property had an old log house, deteriorating outbuildings and no running water or electricity. It was a far cry from a developed ski resort, but the setting suited the life she wanted.Friends helped her make the buildings usable. Woolsey also continued working as a writer, spending winters in New York City as editor of Ski Illustrated, described in her biographical account as America's first magazine devoted to skiing. After three years, she left the position and moved to the ranch permanently.She improved the house, added a barn and acquired more meadowland. What had begun as a modest rural property developed into a guest ranch, with visitors paying to stay and often lending a hand with daily chores. Woolsey's approach combined hospitality with an active outdoor life, rather than treating the ranch simply as accommodation for tourists.A ranch built around horses, skiing and mountain travelTrail Creek Ranch gave Woolsey a base for the activities that had shaped her life. In summer, she led pack trips into the surrounding wilderness, using maps to guide the routes and sometimes relying on trout caught along the way for meals. Local rancher and hunting guide Gibb Scott helped her learn more about horseback travel in the mountains and the practical demands of running a ranch.Protecting the land beyond her lifetimeWoolsey had watched the mountain West change during her own lifetime. In her autobiography, Off the Beaten Track, she reflected on the shrinking availability of uncrowded wilderness and untracked snow, as ski racing became an increasingly commercial enterprise. The changes were personal as well as environmental: the places that had attracted her to Wyoming were becoming harder to find.The conservation easement associated with Trail Creek Ranch helped protect the property's 270 acres from development after decades of use as a working ranch. Rather than leaving the land exposed to the changes Woolsey had observed, the arrangement placed lasting limits on how it could be developed.Woolsey died at Trail Creek Ranch on 11 January 1997, aged 88. The account of her life published by the American Alpine Club recalled her final view of the meadow, horses feeding on snow as evening shadows moved across the property. articles.title: US to livestream Fort Hood shooter’s execution: Is that legal?​
articles.summary: Rights groups and legal experts say the move could endanger minors, who are usually barred from witnessing executions.
articles.body:
The Pentagon has said it will livestream the upcoming execution of convicted mass shooter Nidal Malik Hasan by firing squad – a first for the United States.

A Pentagon spokesperson made the announcement on Thursday, drawing uproar from legal quarters as experts and rights groups raised concerns that it could violate US and international laws and, in particular, put minors at risk.

The US military rarely invokes capital punishment, last executing an officer by hanging in 1961. Firing squads are even rarer, and were last used in the military in 1945.

Nidal Malik Hasan, a then-Army major, opened fire at an Army processing centre in Fort Hood, Texas, on November 5, 2009, killing 13 people and injuring 32 others.

An Army psychiatrist found he was acting in an effort to stop military deployments to Afghanistan and to halt the killing of fellow Muslims. Hasan was himself scheduled to be deployed later that month.

Following a lengthy military trial in which Hasan made little effort to defend himself, a jury convicted him in July 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of murder, and imposed the death penalty.

Although he said he acted on religious grounds and was found to have corresponded with al-Qaeda-linked elements, Hasan was not convicted of “terrorism” as the US military justice code does not have a stand-alone charge for it.

This week, the Pentagon said US President Donald Trump had given the go-ahead for Hasan to face a firing squad. The military requires presidential approval for executions, and only the president can stipulate a particular method.

On Thursday, a Pentagon official said Hasan was to be executed at the same Fort Hood military base where he killed 13 people in 2009.

The official said the execution would be livestreamed.

Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle set the execution date for December 3 at 1pm local time (18:00 GMT).

Speaking in a podcast interview this week, Hegseth said the livestream would act as a deterrent.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said during the interview with far-right podcaster Jack Posobiec.

He added that the timing of the execution was symbolic. “We’re going to do it at one o’clock, which is when he did it, and it’s going to be soldiers with rifles executing the firing squad.”

The rules vary in the 27 US states where death penalties are still in place.

Texas law allows up to five close relatives of the victim, a spiritual guide, justice officials, state-ordained chaplains, a judge, the sheriff, and the media to attend an execution.

All persons, however, must be adults older than 18.

When was the last public execution in the US?

It was on August 14, 1936. Rainey Bethea was publicly hanged in Owensboro, Kentucky, after confessing to the rape and killing of 70-year-old Lishia Edwards.

What does international law say about public executions?

The US is a signatory to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), which bans torture, cruel, inhuman, or degrading punishment.

While the convention does not completely ban the death penalty, it does strictly restrict its use to the “most serious crimes” and encourages its abolition.

Washington ratified it in 1992, but it issued reservations and stated that the US would retain the right to impose capital punishment as it sees fit.

Legal experts say the public execution of Hasan could violate the clause against degrading punishment under the convention. A livestream would likely also be recorded and shared widely.

What does US law say about who can witness executions?

British-American human rights lawyer Clive Stafford Smith, who has represented clients on death row in the US and founded the Louisiana Capital Assistance Center in New Orleans in 1993 to represent low-income individuals facing the death penalty, called the move “barbaric”.

He said a public execution broadcast in this manner would violate several laws in the US that prohibit the transmission of obscene, indecent, or graphic material, especially to minors.

There’s no single federal law stipulating who may witness executions, but death penalty states typically prohibit minors.

Likewise, the Army’s justice code ( PDF ) prohibits minors from witnessing an execution.

“I’ve watched six executions, and I suffer from PTSD [post-traumatic stress disorder] to this day,” Stafford Smith told Al Jazeera. “It’s a nightmare, and you’ll have people who will have traumatic responses to it.”

Smith said several legal challenges are likely, and the Army will likely have to consider several factors if it does go ahead with broadcasting the execution.

Challengers are likely to question how the US military will prevent children from viewing the livestream, and how they will make Hasan’s shooting less ghastly based on the body parts targeted, he said.

Regarding using the public execution as a deterrent, Stafford Smith added the opposite could actually be more likely. He said it could end up “provoking more cases” and that Hasan could be seen as a “martyr” by some.

He added: “This is likely going to Congress. The Democrats will want to stop this. So that will be an interesting battle.”

How have politicians and rights groups responded?

Democrat Senator Chris Murphy called the move “disgusting” and compared it to executions carried out by the Islamic State (ISIL). “I understand that in this country we have the death penalty, but public executions [are] medieval,” he said in an interview with CNN.

Amnesty International Australia said Hegseth’s statements showed an “appalling disregard for human dignity”, and called on Melbourne to intervene.

Meanwhile, New Zealand’s national censor told rights groups urging it to protest that it has no authority to block internet users from viewing the livestream – a sign that governments attempting to restrict access might be hampered.

articles.title: Hurricane Isaias strengthens into Category 3 storm with US in its sights
articles.summary: The major storm is expected to make landfall along the US Gulf Coast later on Friday or early Saturday.
articles.body:
Hurricane Isaias has strengthened into a major Category 3 storm as the Gulf Coast of the United States prepares for potentially “life-threatening” conditions.

The US National Hurricane Center (NHC) said on Friday that Isaias was packing winds in excess of 193kph (120mph) and was expected to continue strengthening over the course of the day. A Category 3 storm, considered a major hurricane by the NHC, is capable of causing devastating damage.

Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season , is expected to make landfall in the US later on Friday or early Saturday between Mobile Bay on the Alabama coast and Choctawhatchee Bay in Florida, the center said.

When it comes ashore, the storm is forecast to weaken quickly as it moves inland into the southern US. But the NHC urged local governments to quickly prepare for the dangerous conditions that Isaias could bring.

“Preparations should be rushed to completion as the weather will go downhill quickly today”, forecasters said. “While the storm is not expected to make landfall at peak intensity, it is likely that Isaias will still be a significant hurricane when it reaches the coast”.

Storm surge as high as 2.7 metres (9 feet) could impact an area extending from the Alabama-Florida border to Grayton Beach, Florida, creating “dangerous” conditions for residents who live along the Gulf shoreline. Isaias is projected to produce 10.1 to 20.3cm of rainfall (4 to 8 inches) across the coast, with possible localised totals of up to 38cm (15 inches).

“This is a life-threatening situation”, the center warned. “Persons located within these areas should take all necessary actions to protect life and property from rising water and the potential for other dangerous conditions.”

States of emergency have been issued by governments in parts of Alabama, Florida and Georgia. Several coastal counties along the Gulf of Mexico have mandatory evacuation orders.

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who has requested an emergency declaration from US President Donald Trump ahead of Isaias’ landfall, warned residents in the state’s panhandle region of potentially significant storm damage.

“But the surge is really what puts a lot of people’s lives in jeopardy if they haven’t heeded evacuation orders, and does the most significant damage from these storms,” DeSantis said. “Everywhere from Pensacola all the way into the Big Bend section of north Florida, you could see storm surge. So please take caution of that.”

“And we always say you hide from the wind, but you run from the water. When the water’s rising and things are happening, it’s a very, very difficult conundrum — and you do not want to be caught in that,” he added.

On Thursday, the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) urged Gulf Coast residents to prepare for the hurricane and said its offices were “fully engaged”.

As of early Friday, the NHC said Isaias was centred about 386km (240 miles) south of Pensacola in Florida and moving north-northeast at 24kph (15 mph).

articles.title: How Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize win sent a message to the world – and Trump
articles.summary: When South African jurist Navi Pillay won this year’s Nobel Peace Prize, a large proportion of the human rights community happened to be gathered at a conference at the Nuremberg Court in Germany, where the landmark trial of Nazi leaders almost 80 years ago laid the foundations for modern international law.
articles.body: When South African jurist Navi Pillay won this year’s Nobel Peace Prize, she happened to be at a conference at the Nuremberg Court in Germany, where the landmark trial of Nazi leaders almost 80 years ago laid the foundations for modern international law. As her colleagues in the human rights community applauded and congratulated the former International Criminal Court (ICC) judge on her win, her first reaction was simply: “Is it true? I thought it must be a joke.” “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with (US President Donald) Trump,” she quipped, a reference to how last year’s winner gave her medal to the US president, before adding “it’s very appropriate that I’m with friends, colleagues, all of whom support human rights.” The work of this community and the international legal order have increasingly come under attack in recent years – a fact the Nobel committee were eager to highlight in their decision to recognize Pillay, 85. By spotlighting Pillay, who has served on several international courts and oversaw a 2025 UN report that concluded that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, the committee said it wanted to “remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace.” Justice is a ‘necessity’ for peace That message was not explicitly directed at any one state. But implicitly, it rebuked those countries – most notably the US – whose actions have weakened international legal institutions. Hours after Pillay’s win, the Trump administration announced fresh sanctions on the ICC, the body established in 2002 to prosecute individuals accused of war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide. The ICC condemned the move as an “assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order,” called on other states to help support the court but emphasized its work would continue. Several of the court’s prosecutors have already been targeted by US sanctions after it issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defense minister Yoav Gallant in 2024. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio even vowed in July to “dismantle” the ICC, accusing it of “waging a war against our country, not with bullets or missiles,” but with “the force of so-called international law.” Without referencing these efforts, the Nobel committee warned that international law is “an absolute necessity” for peace, even if has struggled to hold the world’s most powerful actors responsible for their actions. “History has shown that a world operating without the rule of law is unjust, unwise and inhumane,” the committee continued. “The judges – those who guard the thin red line between order and chaos – are therefore highly deserving of our praise. But today, as these same judges are sanctioned, and their institutions are attacked.” Pillay, who has served as a judge at both major international courts and as the UN human rights chief, embodies many of the values the committee wanted to emphasize. She too warned that international law, the ICC in particular and human rights are under attack, undermining the principle that justice is required for lasting peace. The choice was a brave one, Haakon Gjerløw, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo, told CNN. “It is big political actors that are pushing against some of these institutions, against some of the legal orders.” Choosing an individual, rather than the institutions for which she works, “shows that we as individuals might work towards peace in our different capacities,” Gjerløw added. An anti-apartheid lawyer Born on September 23, 1941, Pillay grew up in a family of Indian Tamil origin in Durban, South Africa, while the country was still under apartheid. Donations from her local community helped her enrol in classes for non-white students at the University of KwaZulu-Natal and it was there that she first came across transcripts of the Nuremberg Trials. They transfixed her, both by demonstrating the idea of countries coming together to pursue criminal justice and as a framework to understand apartheid-era crimes. After graduating, she defended anti-apartheid activists, exposed the torture of political detainees and successfully sued to stop her own detained husband from being tortured. “I won access to lawyers for political prisoners, including Nelson Mandela,” she wrote in a 2021 CNN op-ed. “The first judge’s chambers I entered was my own, in 1995, as the first non-White woman to serve on the High Court.” However, she never served her full term on South Africa’s High Court as she was elected by the UN General Assembly to be a judge on the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, which sought to prosecute those responsible for the Rwandan genocide in 1994. Pillay was instrumental in two significant legal precedents set by that tribunal – firstly, that rape and sexual violence could constitute a crime against humanity and genocide, and secondly, that a defendant could face “charges of incitement to commit genocide purely on the basis of spreading propaganda,” the Nobel committee said. She served as a judge at the ICC from 2003-2008 before being appointed as the UN human rights chief. She is currently a judge at the International Court of Justice in a case where Myanmar has been accused of genocide. The Nobel committee’s decision to award Pillay the peace prize triggered a backlash from Israel on Friday, which has strenuously denied allegations of genocide. Netanyahu condemned the Nobel committee, saying it had “lost its moral compass” and accusing Pillay of “lies.” There has been no reaction yet from Trump, who has made no secret of his desire for the prize. In an impromptu speech in Nuremberg on Friday, Pillay dedicated her Nobel Prize to “all of the survivors of international crimes” and to those defending international criminal justice “whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign. “Perhaps it was meant to be that I was in this historic courtroom 600 where the Nuremberg Trials were held when the announcement was made and I was informed of the award.”

articles.title: Remember Orkut? Its founder wants to bring it back
articles.summary: Orkut's founder is now taking aim at algorithms and AI-generated content.
articles.body:
Orkut , the once-popular social networking platform that shut down more than a decade ago, may finally be making a comeback, as its founder has called on users to help revive it with a renewed focus on friendship, community, and human connection.

In a post on X on Thursday, Orkut Büyükkökten, the founder of the eponymous social network, urged users to visit Orkut.com and add their names in support of bringing it back, as well as invite others to join.

Orkut first debuted in 2004 as a side project by Büyükkökten, 51, while he was at Google. The social network went on to become hugely popular in India and Brazil but later lost ground to Facebook. Google eventually shut it down in September 2014, shifting its focus to other platforms, including Google+ and YouTube.

In a letter published on Orkut.com, Büyükkökten criticized how social media has evolved over the past two decades, particularly the growing influence of algorithms and AI-generated content. “Artificial intelligence is extraordinary technology, but it’s dissolving the one premise that made social networking special and worth building: that there was a person on the other side,” he wrote.

“I know how to get there: we rebuild the internet we first loved. The one with authentic people, real connection, and genuine belonging,” Büyükkökten added.

This is not the first time Büyükkökten has explored a return to social networking. In 2016, two years after Orkut’s shutdown, he launched another social network, Hello, focused on connecting people through shared interests. The platform shut down in 2020 after attracting more than 2 million downloads worldwide, compared with Orkut’s about 300 million active users .

In 2022, Büyükkökten hinted at another social networking venture in a note on Orkut.com, saying that he was “building something new.” He did not offer further details. Two years later, he told WIRED he was working on a social network that would “leverage AI and machine learning” to bring people together and build communities. That platform has yet to launch.

Now, Büyükkökten is asking people to register their support for Orkut’s return. He has, however, not clarified whether a new version of the platform is already in development or whether it will ever launch.

An email sent to Orkut seeking comment from Büyükkökten did not elicit a response.
